  • "Have you finished with the scissors? I need them." (Are you done using them?)
  • "I've finished with this book. You can borrow it now." (I have no more use for it.)

b) To end a romantic relationship with someone:

  • "She finished with him last week." (She ended the relationship.)

c) To be done dealing with someone, often after giving them a reprimand:

  • "I haven't finished with you yet." (I still have more to say to you — usually said in anger or sternness.)

Finish vs. Stop

These two words are easy to confuse, but they mean different things.

  • Stop means you ceased doing something — but not necessarily because you completed it. You might stop because you are tired, interrupted, or giving up.
  • Finish means you completed something — you went all the way to the end.

Compare:

  • "I stopped reading the book." (I put the book down. I may not have finished it.)
  • "I finished reading the book." (I read the whole thing. I am done.)

Finish vs. End

  • End is more neutral and often applies to things that simply reach their conclusion on their own — events, periods of time, situations.
  • Finish often implies an active effort to complete something, or a stronger sense of totality.

Compare:

  • "The war ended." (It came to a conclusion.)
  • "He finished his work." (He actively completed it.)

Though in many cases they overlap, especially for events: "The show ended" and "The show finished" are both natural.

Imagine a jar being filled with water. Finishing the jar means you have poured water all the way to the brim — the jar is completely full, and there is nothing more to add. Whether it's a task, a meal, a conversation, or a career — finish always points to that moment where the last drop has been poured, and everything that was meant to happen has happened.

• Complete a task: "I finished the project."
  • Use up completely: "We finished the food."
  • Come to an end: "The class finishes at noon."
  • Ruin completely: "The scandal finished him."
  • Apply a final surface treatment: "He finished the wood with oil."
  • Finish off → complete the last part / kill what's already weakened
  • Finish up → wrap up the last parts / end up in a situation
  • Finish with → no longer need something / end a relationship
6098: Finished describes something that has reached its final state. But what that "final state" looks like varies — and this word actually carries three distinct, important meanings (plus one specialized one). Knowing all of them will make you fully fluent with this word.
Meaning 1: Completed — all work is done

The most common meaning. Something is "finished" when the process of working on it is over. Nothing more needs to be added, changed, or done to it.

  • "The finished report is on your desk." → The report is complete; no more work needed.
  • "She admired the finished sculpture." → The sculptor has done everything they intended to do.
  • "The finished building opens next month." → Construction is over.

Think of it as the opposite of "unfinished." An unfinished painting still needs more work. A finished painting has been brought to its intended end.

Key nuance — "finished" vs. "complete": These two words are similar but not identical. "Complete" simply means all the necessary parts are present (a complete puzzle has all its pieces). "Finished" means the process of working on something is truly over. A painting can be complete in its composition but still feel unfinished if the artist hasn't applied the final touches. In everyday use, these words often overlap — but "finished" always carries that extra sense of the work being truly, finally done.
Meaning 2: Highly polished, refined, and accomplished

This is the more elevated and sophisticated meaning. Here, "finished" doesn't just mean done — it means perfected. It describes a person or a piece of work that has reached a state of exceptional refinement, skill, and mastery.

  • "She is a finished pianist." → She plays not just with technical skill, but with artistic polish, elegance, and mastery.
  • "His finished prose style impressed every editor." → His writing is not merely competent; it is refined and polished to a high degree.
  • "He had the manners of a finished gentleman." → His manners were impeccably cultivated — not just decent, but truly refined.
  • "The finished product exceeded all expectations." → The final result is not just complete, but impressively well-made.

Here is a helpful way to picture it: imagine polishing a piece of wood — sanding it, buffing it, treating it — over and over until it gleams perfectly. At that point, it is "finished." The same concept applies to a person's skills or a piece of work. Something or someone that has been refined through great care and effort until it reaches a state of mastery is "finished" in this sense.

This is a high compliment. Calling someone "a finished performer" is praising them at the highest level.
Meaning 3: Ruined, defeated, with no future left

In a completely different direction, "finished" can mean that a person — or sometimes an organization — is ruined, defeated, or has no viable future. The "end" here is not a satisfying completion. It is a final, irreversible collapse of prospects.

  • "After the scandal, the politician was finished." → His career is over; there is no recovery.
  • "If we lose this contract, we're finished." → The company will likely collapse.
  • "He's finished in this industry." → No one will hire him or work with him again.

This meaning is often said with a heavy sense of finality — it conveys that there is nothing left. No hope, no second chance, no future.

Notice the crucial contrast with Meaning 1: a finished project is a good thing — it's done. But a finished career is a devastating thing — it's destroyed. The word is the same; the emotional weight is completely opposite. Context makes everything clear.
Meaning 4: Having a surface treatment applied (specialized use)

In technical or trade contexts — particularly in woodworking, construction, and leatherwork — "finished" describes a surface that has had a treatment (such as varnish, stain, paint, or polish) applied to it.

  • "Finished hardwood floors" → Wood floors that have been sanded, treated, and coated with a protective layer.
  • "Finished leather" → Leather that has been treated and polished on its surface.

You'll mostly encounter this in product descriptions, real estate, home improvement, or crafts. It is less common in everyday conversation, but good to know.
How to tell which meaning is in play

Since the word carries multiple meanings, context is everything. A reliable guide:

  • Describing a completed task, project, or object → Meaning 1 (a finished essay, the finished house)
  • Describing a person's level of skill or the quality of a work → Meaning 2 (a finished musician, finished writing)
  • Describing a person or organization whose future has collapsed → Meaning 3 (she's finished, the company is finished)
  • Describing a treated material surface in a trade context → Meaning 4 (finished floors, finished wood)

In practice, you will almost never be confused — the surrounding sentence will tell you immediately which sense is meant.
The single thread connecting all meanings

Every meaning of "finished" as an adjective traces back to the same core idea: something has been brought to its ultimate end. Whether that end is a satisfying completion, a state of polished mastery, a collapse of all prospects, or a surface made ready for use — the common thread is that there is no further progress possible. The process is over. What you see is the final form.

That is "finished" — entirely and completely.
6099:
Finite means having a limit. Something finite has a definite end, a definite boundary, or a definite amount. It does not go on forever. It is not unlimited.

A simple test: if you can — at least in theory — count something, measure it, or reach the end of it, then it is finite.
The Clearest Way to Picture It

Imagine a glass of water. It holds a specific amount — say, 250 ml. That's it. No more. That glass of water is finite. Now imagine a magical glass that refills endlessly and never runs out. That would be infinite — the direct opposite of finite.

The word infinite is the exact opposite of finite. Infinite means having no limit, no boundary, and no end — going on forever. These two words are mirror images of each other, so understanding one instantly helps you understand the other.

A book is finite — it has a last page. The concept of numbers, however, is infinite — you can always add one more and never truly reach the "last" number.

Time. Human life is finite. You are born, you live, and eventually your life ends. A day has only 24 hours — a finite amount of time. This is why people say things like "our time is finite, so use it wisely."

Resources. Oil, coal, and natural gas are finite resources — the Earth holds a fixed supply, and once used up, they are gone. The money in your wallet is finite. The food in your fridge is finite.

Space. A room has a finite amount of space. A hard drive has a finite amount of storage. A parking lot has a finite number of spots.

Quantities. A finite number of anything simply means a specific, countable amount — not endless. A library might have a finite number of books. A city has a finite number of people.
A Critical Nuance: Finite Does Not Mean Small

This is where many learners make a mistake. Finite does not mean "small" or "few." It simply means "not infinite."

A number can be astronomically large — a trillion trillion trillion — and still be perfectly finite, because it is a definite, reachable amount. Infinite, by contrast, can never be reached. No matter how large a finite number grows, infinity is always larger.

So when you hear "finite," think limited — not necessarily tiny.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Finite carries a quiet philosophical weight that goes beyond its dictionary meaning. When someone says "life is finite" or "our resources are finite," they are not just stating a neutral fact — they are reminding us that something valuable will eventually run out. This gives the word a sense of urgency and preciousness.

Because of this, "finite" frequently appears in conversations about time management (don't waste your finite energy), environmentalism (finite natural resources), mortality (a finite human lifespan), and decision-making (you have a finite number of chances). The underlying message is almost always the same: this will not last forever, so treat it with care.

In mathematics, "finite" has a very precise meaning. A finite set is a collection that contains a specific, countable number of elements. The set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} is finite — it has exactly 5 elements and then stops. By contrast, the set of all even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8, 10... going on without end) is an infinite set.

Mathematicians also speak of finite sequences (a list of numbers that ends), finite series (a sum that has a definite last term), and finite groups (mathematical structures with a specific number of members). In every case, "finite" is doing the same job: saying that something is bounded and does not go on forever.

In grammar, a finite verb is a verb that is anchored — limited — to a specific subject and a specific tense. In the sentence "She runs every morning," the word runs is a finite verb. It is tied to a particular person (she) and a particular time (present tense).

Compare this to non-finite verbs, like infinitives (to run) or participles (running), which are not locked to any specific subject or tense. They float freely. Finite verbs, however, are committed — they have limits, just like the word suggests.

In computing, you may encounter phrases like finite state machine or finite automaton. These refer to systems that can only ever exist in one of a fixed, limited number of conditions or "states" at any given time. A traffic light, for example, is a simple finite state machine — it can only be in one of three states: red, yellow, or green. There is no fourth option; the system is bounded. "Finite" here, once again, means: not unlimited, not open-ended.

Finite = having a limit, a boundary, or an end. Not infinite. Not endless.

Whenever you encounter this word, ask yourself: "Does this have a definite end or a maximum amount?" If yes — it's finite. Whether you're reading about time, money, natural resources, mathematics, grammar, or computer science, the word is always anchoring something to the idea of this much, and no more.
